finding.claim: The graphql-transport-ws WebSocket handler executes client operations without passing allowed_operation_types, so mutations run over WebSocket even though the HTTP GET path restricts operation types. Mutations are not limited to POST, and the GET restriction is not applied to the WebSocket transport.
finding.source: Client message over a graphql-transport-ws WebSocket (subscribe payload: query, variables, operationName). Entry point: any integration's WebSocket route that negotiates the graphql-transport-ws subprotocol.
finding.sink: self.schema.stream(...) at handlers.py:254, which executes mutation resolvers.

trace.note: run_operation calls schema.stream(query, variable_values, context_value, root_value, operation_name) with no allowed_operation_types argument.
stream() sets allowed_operation_types = DEFAULT_ALLOWED_OPERATION_TYPES when None.
The operation-type check passes for MUTATION, so the mutation executes.
Contrast: HTTP path derives allowed types from the HTTP method, via OperationType.from_http and the allow_queries_via_get check at lines 198-199.
Contrast: from_http('GET') returns only QUERY and SUBSCRIPTION (lines 17-22); POST also allows MUTATION (lines 24-29).
Contrast: the legacy graphql-ws protocol calls schema.subscribe, which restricts to SUBSCRIPTION (schema.py:1240).

finding.guards_checked: Operation-type check (schema.py:709/747) runs but permits MUTATION. No transport-level filter in graphql_transport_ws/handlers.py (grep for OperationType/allowed_operation returned nothing there). No Origin check (see F2). No CSRF token check on WebSocket. Resolver-level permission classes still apply, but they are developer-defined and typically only check the session user, which a cross-site attacker would be using. Not verified dynamically; traced by reading. It is possible mutations over WS are an intentional feature. The inconsistency with the GET/POST restriction is the concern.

finding.claim: No WebSocket upgrade in any integration validates the Origin header, so a cross-site page can open an authenticated WebSocket if the browser sends the session cookie. With F1, that yields state-changing mutations; on the legacy graphql-ws path it yields read access to subscriptions only.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled web page at another origin running new WebSocket(victimGraphqlUrl) with the victim's browser. The victim must be logged in and the browser must attach the session cookie to the cross-site WebSocket handshake.
finding.sink: request.accept(...) followed by the GraphQL-over-WebSocket handler, which builds context from the cookie-authenticated session and runs operations (see F1 for mutations).

trace.note: create_websocket_response calls request.accept(subprotocol=...) at line 217 with no Origin check. is_websocket_request/pick_websocket_subprotocol (203-212) only check scope type and subprotocol.
Same pattern: accept at line 317 with no Origin check.
Same pattern: accept at line 190 (no Origin validation, and no Channels AllowedHostsOriginValidator is applied by the library).
Same pattern in the Django view's create_websocket_response.
Base hook is_websocket_request defined without any origin logic. Other integrations (aiohttp, flask, quart, sanic, litestar) follow the same pattern.

finding.guards_checked: Searched all of strawberry/ for origin/Origin/allowed_origins/check_origin: no matches in any HTTP, WebSocket, or framework integration. Exploitability depends on the app's cookie config: a SameSite=Lax or Strict session cookie is generally not sent on cross-site WebSocket handshakes (Django's default SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE is Lax, which limits this). SameSite=None cookies, or an attacker on a sibling subdomain (same-site), would be sent. Not verified in a browser.

finding.claim: The Channels HTTP handler has no CSRF protection of its own. Django's CsrfViewMiddleware does not run in the Channels ASGI path, so a multipart/form-data POST carrying a mutation is accepted with cookie auth when multipart uploads are enabled.
finding.source: Cross-site HTML form or fetch POST with Content-Type multipart/form-data, fields operations and map, sent by a victim's browser with cookies.
finding.sink: parse_multipart -> replace_placeholders_with_files, then execute_operation, which runs a mutation (POST allows MUTATION per types/graphql.py:24-29).

trace.note: MultiPartParser parses the body from the consumer, with no CSRF check. The form field 'operations' is read at line 113.
parse_http_body accepts multipart only when self.multipart_uploads_enabled is set (line 584).
multipart_uploads_enabled defaults to False, so this is opt-in.
Sync Django view has no csrf_exempt, so Django's middleware still enforces CSRF there. The gap is specific to the Channels path.

finding.guards_checked: Content-Type restriction: JSON POSTs cannot be sent cross-site without a CORS preflight, so only multipart is exposed. multipart_uploads_enabled defaults to False. Cookie SameSite default (Lax) generally blocks cross-site POST cookies, so this needs SameSite=None or a same-site attacker. Low confidence and low impact; included for completeness.
